lecture.title: Esophagus I: Surgical Anatomy, Physiology, Esophageal Emergencies, GERD and Hiatus Hernia
golden_tip: Surgical (subcutaneous) emphysema after vomiting is virtually pathognomonic for esophageal perforation - treat as Boerhaave until proven otherwise, not myocardial infarction.
Boerhaave is the most serious esophageal perforation: full-thickness barotrauma drives gastric content into the mediastinum and pleura - rapid chemical irritation, then fatal infection if untreated.
Beware button batteries in the esophagus: they burn and perforate within hours - urgent endoscopic removal, never observation.
Severity of GERD symptoms often fails to match the severity of erosive esophagitis, and many Barrett's patients are asymptomatic - endoscope whenever alarm features appear.
Types II-IV hiatus hernia can volvulize, obstruct and strangulate; repair = reduce the hernia, resect the sac, close the hiatal defect. Type I is managed like GERD.

sections.heading: Gross Anatomy, Landmarks and Lecture Objectives
sections.body_text:
The lecture sets four objectives: to understand the surgical anatomy and physiology of the esophagus, to assess how to evaluate patients with esophageal diseases, to understand how trauma affects the esophagus, and to build a rational approach to patients with benign and malignant esophageal diseases.

The esophagus is a **muscular tube connecting the pharynx to the stomach**. It measures **23-25 cm in length** and contains **two sphincters**, an upper esophageal sphincter (UES) and a lower esophageal sphincter (LES). It is **lined by squamous epithelium** (stratified, non-keratinizing) and only a short segment, **less than 3 cm, lies below the diaphragm** as the intra-abdominal esophagus. Although conceptually a simple conduit, the structure and function of the esophagus are considerably more complex than a plain tube: it coordinates bolus transport, barrier function at both ends, and clearance of refluxate, all without a serosal cover for most of its length.
key_points: Esophagus = muscular tube from pharynx to stomach, 23-25 cm long.
Contains two sphincters: upper (UES) and lower (LES).
Lined by stratified squamous epithelium; less than 3 cm lies below the diaphragm.
Lecture objectives: anatomy and physiology, patient assessment, trauma effects, approach to benign and malignant disease.

sections.heading: Sites of External Compression and Clinical Relevance
sections.body_text:
Three structures indent and externally compress the esophageal lumen at predictable points:
- The **aorta** (impression of the arch and descending thoracic aorta).
- The **left main stem bronchus**.
- The **diaphragm** (the hiatal narrowing at the diaphragmatic hiatus).

These are the narrowest points of the esophageal lumen and therefore the levels at which swallowed objects slow down or lodge. The lecture stresses a direct **clinical application in foreign body impaction**: coins, food boluses and, most dangerously, **button batteries** typically impact at one of these three compressions, so the radiograph of any impacted foreign body must be interpreted with these levels in mind.
key_points: External compression sites: aorta, left main stem bronchus, diaphragm.
These three narrowings are the classic impaction points for foreign bodies.
Radiographs of impacted objects should be read against these levels.

sections.heading: Histology of the Esophageal Wall
sections.body_text:
From lumen outward, the esophageal wall has these layers:
- **Mucosa** - composed of **stratified squamous epithelium**, **lamina propria** and **muscularis mucosa**.
- **Submucosa** - loose connective tissue containing the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, mucus glands and vessels.
- **Muscularis propria** - **skeletal muscle in the upper one third** and **smooth muscle in the lower two thirds**; this mixed arrangement explains why the cervical esophagus is under volitional control, while the thoracic and abdominal segments are autonomically driven.
- **Adventitia** - an outer fibroelastic coat. The esophagus has **no serosa and no mesentery** along most of its length, which is surgically decisive: it weakens suture-holding and permits rapid spread of infection and tumor into the mediastinum.
key_points: Mucosa: stratified squamous epithelium + lamina propria + muscularis mucosa.
Muscularis propria: skeletal muscle upper 1/3, smooth muscle lower 2/3.
Adventitia only - no serosal covering over most of the esophagus.
Absence of serosa favors early mediastinal spread of infection and cancer.

sections.heading: Innervation and Neurotransmitters
sections.body_text:
Esophageal innervation is predominantly **vagal**. The **vagus nerve supplies the smooth muscle** of the lower two thirds, while the striated muscle of the upper third receives its motor input through the recurrent laryngeal branches of the vagus and the glossopharyngeal nerve. Two intrinsic plexuses run within the wall:
- The **myenteric (Auerbach) plexus**, lying between the circular and longitudinal muscle coats, which generates and coordinates **peristalsis**.
- The **Meissner's (submucosal) plexus**, which regulates secretion and submucosal blood flow.

The key neurotransmitters are functionally polarized: **acetylcholine (ACh) is excitatory and predominates proximally**, whereas **nitric oxide (NO) is inhibitory and predominates distally**. Loss of the distal inhibitory neurons (as in achalasia) abolishes LES relaxation; loss of proximal excitatory drive (as in scleroderma) strips the esophagus of propulsive power.
key_points: Vagus nerve supplies the smooth-muscle (lower 2/3) esophagus.
Myenteric plexus drives peristalsis; Meissner plexus is submucosal.
ACh = excitatory, proximal; NO = inhibitory, distal.
Achalasia = loss of distal inhibitory neurons; scleroderma = loss of excitatory drive.

sections.heading: Blood Supply - Segmental Orientation
sections.body_text:
The esophageal blood supply follows a **segmental orientation**, matching its three topographic segments, and each segment shares its vessels with **other viscera**:
- **Cervical esophagus** - inferior thyroid arteries (shared with the thyroid gland).
- **Thoracic esophagus** - bronchial arteries and multiple small direct branches from the descending thoracic aorta.
- **Abdominal esophagus** - left gastric artery (a celiac trunk branch shared with the stomach) and the inferior phrenic arteries.

Venous drainage parallels the arteries: the cervical and thoracic segments drain to the brachiocephalic and azygos/hemiazygos systems, while the abdominal segment drains via the left gastric vein into the portal system. This creates the **portal-systemic anastomosis at the distal esophagus**, the seat of esophageal varices in portal hypertension. The rich intramural anastomotic network explains why esophageal anastomoses generally heal well and why ischemic strictures of the esophagus are uncommon.
key_points: Segmental supply: inferior thyroid (cervical), bronchial/aortic branches (thoracic), left gastric and inferior phrenic (abdominal).
Left gastric venous drainage creates the portal-systemic anastomosis - the variceal zone.
Rich intramural collaterals explain good anastomotic healing.

concepts.title: Esophageal Physiology: Peristalsis and the Two Sphincters
concepts.summary_ar: يشرح هذا المفهوم فيزيولوجيا المريء: المعج الأولي المطلق ببلعة الطعام والمنقبض من الأعلى إلى الأسفل، والثانوي المطلق بتمدد المريء والارتجاع لتنظيف التجويف، والانقباضات الثالثة غير الدافعة، والعاصرة العلوية من العضلة الحلقية البلعومية المنقبضة نبريا في الراحة، والعاصرة السفلية بضغط 10-40 ملم زئبق كعاصرة فسيولوجية تعمل مع الحجاب الحاجز.

sections.heading: Patterns of Esophageal Peristalsis
sections.body_text:
Esophageal motor activity takes three recognizable patterns:
- **Primary peristalsis** - initiated by the **food bolus**; a progressive contraction wave that travels **from proximal to distal**, carrying the swallowed bolus into the stomach. It is the contraction sequence of the voluntary swallow.
- **Secondary peristalsis** - triggered by **esophageal distention (a residual food bolus) and by reflux**; it is a clearance reflex that strips retained material and refluxate back into the stomach without a new swallow.
- **Tertiary contractions** - non-propulsive, uncoordinated contractions of the esophageal body. They serve no transport function and are common incidental manometric and radiologic findings, becoming frequent with aging and prominent in diffuse esophageal spasm.

Together, peristaltic amplitude and the sequenced relaxation of the two sphincters guarantee bolus transport and esophageal emptying; failure of this machinery produces dysphagia and stasis rather than pain alone.
key_points: Primary peristalsis: food bolus, contraction travels proximal to distal.
Secondary peristalsis: esophageal distention (residual bolus) and reflux - the clearance reflex.
Tertiary contractions: non-propulsive, uncoordinated, common with aging.

options: Primary peristalsis
Secondary peristalsis
Tertiary contractions

check.explanation_ar: المعج الثانوي يُطلقه تمدد المريء ببقايا الطعام أو الارتجاع لتنظيف التجويف دون بلعة جديدة، بينما الأولي يتبع البلع مباشرة والثالث غير دافع.

sections.heading: Upper Esophageal Sphincter (UES)
sections.body_text:
The **upper esophageal sphincter is composed of the cricopharyngeus muscle** - the transverse fibers attached to the cricoid cartilage that close the pharyngoesophageal junction.
- **At rest it is in a state of tonic contraction** (tonic contracture), which prevents inspired air from entering the esophagus and protects the airway from aspirated esophageal content.
- **During the pharyngeal phase of swallowing it relaxes** precisely for the fraction of a second needed for the bolus to pass from pharynx to esophagus, then closes again before the propulsive wave arrives.

Failure of timed cricopharyngeal relaxation (cricopharyngeal achalasia, Zenker diverticulum) produces dysphagia felt high in the neck, while weakness of UES closure predisposes to aspiration pneumonia.
key_points: UES = cricopharyngeus muscle.
Rest: tonic contraction (guards the airway).
Pharyngeal phase of swallowing: timed relaxation.

sections.heading: Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES) - the Physiological Sphincter
sections.body_text:
The **lower esophageal sphincter** is defined by function rather than by anatomy:
- Its resting pressure is **10-40 mm Hg** above intragastric pressure.
- It lies **below the diaphragm**, at the top of the short intra-abdominal esophageal segment (less than 3 cm).
- It is a **physiological sphincter, not a true anatomic sphincter** - no distinct anatomical ring exists; the high-pressure zone is created by the thickened circular muscle of the distal esophagus together with the pinchcock effect of the diaphragmatic crura and the mucosal rosette at the cardia.
- The LES **normally works in conjunction with the diaphragm** to form the primary antireflux barrier - a relationship revisited in GERD and hiatus hernia.

Transient LES relaxations that are not triggered by swallowing are the dominant mechanism allowing reflux episodes in both healthy people and GERD patients.
key_points: LES resting pressure: 10-40 mm Hg.
Located below the diaphragm; physiological, not a true anatomic sphincter.
Works in conjunction with the diaphragm as the main antireflux barrier.
Transient LES relaxations are the dominant reflux mechanism.

options: 0-5 mm Hg

60-90 mm Hg

المعج الثانوي الذي يُطلقه تمدد المريء ببقايا الطعام أو الارتجاع، ووظيفته تنظيف تجويف المريء دون بلعة جديدة.

concepts.title: Esophageal Testing and Symptom Assessment
concepts.summary_ar: يستعرض هذا المفهوم اختبارات المريء الأربعة: بلع الباريوم والتنظير المرن أو الصلب وقياس الضغط داخل التجويف ورصد الحموضة على مدار 24 ساعة، مع مؤشرات التنظير ودور قياس الضغط في اضطرابات الحركة، ثم تقييم الأعراض النموذجية كالحرقة وعسر البلع والارتجاع، والأعراض غير النموذجية كبحة الصوت والسعال والرائحة الكريهة.

sections.heading: The Four Core Esophageal Tests
sections.body_text:
Esophageal testing rests on four complementary investigations:
- **Barium swallow** - a contrast radiograph of swallowing that defines anatomy: strictures, diverticula, hiatal hernia, extrinsic compression, leaks and fistulae.
- **Endoscopy** - direct mucosal and structural inspection, with biopsy and therapeutic capability.
- **Manometry** - intraluminal pressure measurement of the sphincters and peristaltic function.
- **24-hour pH monitoring** - continuous (ambulatory) measurement of acid exposure in the esophagus over a full day-night cycle, correlating symptoms with reflux episodes.

The sequence chosen depends on the working diagnosis: structural questions go to barium swallow and endoscopy first, whereas functional questions go to manometry and pH monitoring.
key_points: Four tests: barium swallow, endoscopy, manometry, 24-hour pH monitoring.
Barium swallow and endoscopy answer structural questions.
Manometry and pH monitoring answer functional questions.

sections.heading: Endoscopy: Evaluation and Indications
sections.body_text:
Endoscopy (esophagoscopy, or upper GI endoscopy/EGD) evaluates:
- The **mucosa** (esophagitis, Barrett metaplasia, mucosal tears, tumors).
- **Structural abnormalities** (strictures, webs, rings, extrinsic compression, hiatal hernia).
- It may be **rigid or flexible**; flexible instruments dominate modern practice, while rigid esophagoscopy retains a role for some impacted foreign bodies.
- It is **diagnostic and/or therapeutic** (dilation, injection of bleeding lesions, foreign body retrieval, stenting).

**Indications for endoscopy** in esophageal disease:
- **Weight loss**.
- **Upper gastrointestinal bleeding**.
- **Dysphagia, odynophagia and chest pain** of esophageal origin.
- **Partial or no response to empiric therapy** - a warning that the symptomatic diagnosis is wrong.
- **Evaluation for Barrett's esophagus** in chronic reflux.
key_points: Evaluates mucosa and structural abnormalities; rigid or flexible; diagnostic and/or therapeutic.
Indications: weight loss, upper GI bleeding, dysphagia/odynophagia/chest pain.
Partial or no response to empiric therapy mandates endoscopy.
Evaluation for Barrett's esophagus is a standing indication in chronic GERD.

sections.heading: Manometry - Measuring Esophageal Motor Function
sections.body_text:
Esophageal manometry **measures intraluminal pressures** along the esophagus and thereby demonstrates:
- The **coordination of the pressure activities of the LES, the esophageal body and the UES** during swallowing.
- Resting sphincter pressures, peristaltic amplitude, wave progression and completeness of deglutitive relaxation.

Its main indication is the **assessment of patients with symptoms suggestive of esophageal motor dysfunction**, classically:
- **Achalasia** - absent peristalsis with a hypertensive, non-relaxing LES.
- **Scleroderma** - low LES pressure with feeble, aperistaltic smooth-muscle segments (the inverse pattern).

Manometry is also essential before antireflux surgery, to exclude a misdiagnosed motility disorder, and during 24-hour pH studies, to position the pH electrode 5 cm above the manometrically defined LES.
key_points: Manometry measures intraluminal pressures.
Shows coordination of LES, esophageal body and UES pressure activity.
Key indications: suspected motor dysfunction - achalasia, scleroderma.
Mandatory before antireflux surgery and for pH-catheter positioning.

sections.heading: Typical (Classic) Esophageal Symptoms
sections.body_text:
The five typical esophageal symptoms are:
- **Heartburn** - retrosternal burning rising toward the throat; the cardinal reflux symptom.
- **Dysphagia** - the **sensation of food being delayed in its normal passage from mouth to stomach**; patients often complain of a sensation of food 'sticking'. Note that dysphagia is a transit symptom, not merely pain.
- **Odynophagia** - painful swallowing, typical of severe esophagitis, pill-induced injury, infection or neoplasia.
- **Regurgitation** - effortless return of esophageal or gastric content into the mouth or pharynx, without nausea or retching.
- **Aspiration** - entry of refluxed material into the airway, causing nocturnal cough, choking or pneumonia.

The combination of typical symptoms with risk factors usually allows a working diagnosis before any test is ordered.
key_points: Heartburn, dysphagia, odynophagia, regurgitation, aspiration = the five typical symptoms.
Dysphagia = sensation of food delayed/sticking in its passage from mouth to stomach.
Aspiration = refluxate entering the airway (nocturnal cough, choking, pneumonia).

sections.heading: Atypical Esophageal Symptoms
sections.body_text:
Esophageal disease - especially reflux - frequently presents outside the retrosternal territory. Atypical symptoms include:
- **Dyspepsia** (epigastric burning and fullness).
- **Nausea and vomiting**.
- **Hematemesis** (haematemesis).
- **Globus** - the sensation of a lump in the throat with no structural obstruction.
- **Coughing**, **throat clearing** and **throat pain**.
- **Hoarseness** (reflux laryngitis).
- **Wheezing/stridor** and **dyspnea** (reflux-triggered bronchospasm).
- **Apnea** (reflux-associated apneic spells in infants).
- **Halitosis**.

Because these symptoms overlap with respiratory, ENT and cardiac disease, a high index of suspicion is required; complications of GERD may appear in patients who never had typical heartburn.
key_points: Atypical list: dyspepsia, nausea/vomiting, hematemesis, globus, cough, throat clearing, throat pain, hoarseness, wheezing/stridor, dyspnea, apnea, halitosis.
GERD complications can appear without typical symptoms.
Respiratory and ENT presentations of reflux are common and easily missed.

concepts.title: Esophageal Emergencies: Foreign Bodies, Perforation and Mallory-Weiss Syndrome
concepts.summary_ar: يتناول هذا المفهوم طوارئ المريء: الأجسام الأجنبية وأشيعها بلعة الطعام الدالة على مرض كامن مع خطر بطاريات الأزرار، والانثقاب العلاجي المنشأ أو التلقائي الانضغاطي (متلازمة بورهاف) الذي يظل الانتفاخ الجراحي علامته شبه المميزة مع فخ التشخيص الخاطئ كجلطة قلبية، وقرار العلاج الجراحي أو التحفظي وفق أربعة عوامل، ومتلازمة مالوري-ويس النزفية.

sections.heading: Foreign Bodies in the Esophagus
sections.body_text:
Foreign body entrapment is a common esophageal emergency.
- The **most common esophageal foreign body is a food bolus** (typically meat impaction), and its importance is that it **usually signifies underlying disease** - a stricture, ring, web or tumor that has narrowed the lumen. A bolus impaction in an adult therefore mandates later endoscopic evaluation of the esophagus even after successful clearance.
- **It is usually possible to remove foreign bodies by flexible or rigid endoscopy** under sedation or anesthesia; blind instrumental pushing, bougienage of an unrecognized obstruction and forced emesis are discouraged.
- **Beware of button batteries in the oesophagus**: a lodged disc generates hydroxide at its negative pole and burns the mucosa within hours, producing deep necrosis, perforation and even aortoesophageal fistula. A battery seen on x-ray within the esophagus is an indication for **urgent endoscopic removal**, never for observation.
- Impaction occurs at the **three sites of external compression** (aorta, left main stem bronchus, diaphragm).

Button batteries, sharp objects and multiple magnets all warrant same-session urgent removal rather than watchful waiting.
key_points: Most common foreign body: food bolus - usually signifies underlying disease.
Removal is usually possible by flexible or rigid endoscopy.
Beware button batteries - burns and perforation within hours; urgent removal.
Impaction happens at the three compression sites.

options: Observe with repeat x-ray in 24 hours
Discharge home awaiting spontaneous passage

Induce vomiting to expel the battery

sections.heading: Perforation: Etiology and Boerhaave Syndrome (Barotrauma)
sections.body_text:
Perforation of the oesophagus is **usually iatrogenic (at therapeutic endoscopy)** - dilation, variceal therapy, foreign body retrieval, stenting - **or due to 'barotrauma' (spontaneous perforation)**.

**Barotrauma (spontaneous perforation, Boerhaave syndrome):**
- This occurs **classically when a person vomits against a closed glottis**. The pressure in the oesophagus **increases rapidly**, and the oesophagus **bursts at its weakest point in the lower third**, sending a **stream of material into the mediastinum and often the pleural cavity as well**.
- **Boerhaave syndrome is the most serious type of perforation. WHY? Because it is a full-thickness barometric rupture of a healthy wall**: it causes **rapid chemical irritation in the mediastinum and pleura followed by infection if untreated** - fulminant mediastinitis, empyema and septic shock. Instrumental perforations, by contrast, are often recognized immediately, occur in a prepared patient and are frequently contained.
- The lecture asks: what factors enhance the spread of gastro-intestinal fluid to the mediastinum? The **negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration actively sucks fluid out** through the tear, while continued swallowing keeps feeding the leak; a full stomach and ongoing vomiting enlarge the delivered volume.
- Barotrauma has also been described in relation to **other pressure events** - straining, weightlifting, childbirth, compressed-air exposure and forceful Valsalva maneuvers.

**Surgical emphysema is virtually pathognomonic**: subcutaneous air with swelling, bruising, dusky discoloration and crepitus in the neck and supraclavicular areas - the key teaching finding of the lecture's clinical photograph. Many instrumental perforations can be managed conservatively, but spontaneous perforation is often life-threatening.
key_points: Perforation is usually iatrogenic (therapeutic endoscopy) or barotrauma (spontaneous).
Boerhaave: vomiting against a closed glottis; burst at the weakest point of the lower third; contents enter mediastinum and often pleura.
Most serious type: rapid chemical irritation then infection - mediastinitis, empyema, septic shock.
Negative intrathoracic pressure enhances spread of gastro-intestinal fluid into the mediastinum.
Surgical emphysema is virtually pathognomonic; spontaneous perforation is often life-threatening.

sections.heading: Diagnosis of Spontaneous Perforation - the Classic Pitfalls
sections.body_text:
The **clinical history is usually severe pain in the chest or upper abdomen following a meal or a bout of drinking**, with **associated shortness of breath common**.

Pitfalls stressed by the lecture:
- **Many cases are misdiagnosed as myocardial infarction, perforated peptic ulcer or pancreatitis** when the pain is confined to the upper abdomen - three mimics that delay a life-saving diagnosis.
- There may be a **surprising amount of rigidity on examination of the upper abdomen, even in the absence of any peritoneal contamination** - the rigidity is referred from diaphragmatic and mediastinal irritation, so a 'surgical abdomen' without free contamination is still consistent with Boerhaave.
- Supporting signs: **surgical (subcutaneous) emphysema** in the neck and supraclavicular fossae, fever, tachycardia, hypoxia, left pleural effusion and mediastinal widening on chest x-ray, and rapid deterioration toward septic shock.

Any severe chest or upper abdominal pain after vomiting, plus surgical emphysema, is Boerhaave until proven otherwise.
key_points: History: severe chest/upper abdominal pain after a meal or bout of drinking; shortness of breath common.
Classic misdiagnoses: myocardial infarction, perforated peptic ulcer, pancreatitis.
Surprising upper abdominal rigidity may occur without any peritoneal contamination.
Surgical emphysema + postemetic pain = Boerhaave until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: Other Types of Perforation
sections.body_text:
Beyond instrumentation and barotrauma:
- **Pathological perforation** - **rare**. What is more common is **erosion into an adjacent structure with fistula formation**; the **aerodigestive (tracheo-broncho-esophageal) fistula is the most common** variety and is usually encountered in **primary malignant disease of the oesophagus or bronchus** (also after radiotherapy or in chronic infectious disease).
- **Penetrating injury** - perforation by **knives and bullets is uncommon, even in war**, because the oesophagus is a **relatively small target surrounded by other vital organs** (heart, great vessels, trachea) that are usually injured first.
- **Foreign bodies** - the oesophagus may be **perforated during removal of a foreign body**, or occasionally by **an object that has been left in the oesophagus for several days** and erodes through the wall (button batteries, sharp bones, pressure necrosis from coins).

Cervical odynophagia, neck induration and fever after instrumentation or foreign body impaction suggest a contained cervical leak - the most forgiving perforation, because the cervical esophagus is surrounded by fascial planes that localize contamination.
key_points: Pathological perforation is rare; erosion with fistula formation is more common.
Aerodigestive fistula is the most common pathological fistula - usually in esophageal or bronchial malignancy.
Penetrating injury is uncommon even in war: small target surrounded by vital organs.
Foreign bodies perforate during removal or after being left several days.

sections.heading: Treatment of Esophageal Perforation - Aim and the Four-Factor Decision
sections.body_text:
**The aim of treatment is to limit mediastinal contamination and to prevent or deal with infection.** All decisions flow from this aim: nothing oral, broad-spectrum antibiotics, drainage of contaminated spaces, and repair or diversion of the leak.

**The decision between operative and non-operative management rests on four factors:**
1. The **site of the perforation** (cervical versus thoracoabdominal oesophagus).
2. The **event causing the perforation** (spontaneous versus instrumental).
3. The **underlying pathology** (benign or malignant).
4. The **interval since perforation and the resulting septic load** - the source slide is truncated after factor 3, and the standard fourth consideration taught alongside this table is the delay before diagnosis and treatment, which governs the degree of mediastinal contamination and physiological derangement.

The lecture presents this decision as a two-column table of factors influencing management of esophageal perforation.

**Factors that favour non-operative management:**
- Small septic load.
- Minimal cardiovascular upset.
- Perforation confined to the mediastinum.
- Perforation by flexible endoscope.
- Perforation of the cervical oesophagus.

**Factors that favour operative repair:**
- Large septic load.
- Septic shock.
- Pleura breached.
- Boerhaave's syndrome.
- Perforation of the abdominal oesophagus.

Non-operative care means nil per os, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, acid suppression, nutritional support (feeding jejunostomy) and drainage of collections if needed. Operative care means primary repair with buttressing, mediastinal toilet, drainage and feeding access; esophagectomy or diversion is reserved for an unsalvageable esophagus.
key_points: Aim: limit mediastinal contamination and prevent or treat infection.
Four factors: site, event, underlying pathology, interval/degree of contamination.
Non-operative: small septic load, minimal upset, confined to mediastinum, flexible endoscope, cervical esophagus.
Operative: large septic load, septic shock, pleura breached, Boerhaave, abdominal esophagus.

check.prompt: Which combination of findings favors OPERATIVE repair of an esophageal perforation?
options: Small septic load with minimal cardiovascular upset
Perforation confined to the mediastinum by flexible endoscope
Septic shock with pleura breached after forceful vomiting
Cervical perforation by flexible endoscope
Minimal contamination with a delayed but contained leak

sections.heading: Lacerations - Mallory-Weiss Syndrome
sections.body_text:
**Mallory-Weiss syndrome** consists of **longitudinal tears in the esophagus at the esophagogastric junction**.
- The **presumed pathogenesis is inadequate relaxation of the musculature of the lower esophageal sphincter during vomiting**, with **stretching and tearing of the esophagogastric junction at the moment of propulsive expulsion** of gastric content - forceful vomiting produces a **mucosal tear at the cardia rather than a full perforation**.
- **Vigorous vomiting produces a vertical split in the gastric mucosa immediately below the squamocolumnar junction at the cardia in 90 per cent of cases** (the lecture's endoscopic image shows exactly this linear laceration, with arrows marking its edges and depth).
- The condition **presents with haematemesis**, classically after initial non-bloody vomiting or retching (alcohol binge, hyperemesis gravidarum).
- **Usually the bleeding is not severe** and settles with supportive care; **endoscopic injection therapy may be required for the occasional severe case**; **surgery is rarely required**.

Distinguish Mallory-Weiss from Boerhaave: Mallory-Weiss is a **partial-thickness mucosal laceration that bleeds**, whereas Boerhaave is a **full-thickness rupture that contaminates the mediastinum** - the same act of vomiting can produce either.
key_points: Longitudinal mucosal tears at the esophagogastric junction - not a full perforation.
Mechanism: inadequate LES relaxation during vomiting with stretching and tearing at propulsive expulsion.
Vertical split in gastric mucosa immediately below the squamocolumnar junction at the cardia in 90% of cases.
Presents with hematemesis; bleeding usually not severe; endoscopic injection if severe; surgery rare.

check.prompt: Where does the Mallory-Weiss laceration characteristically occur?
options: Upper third of the esophagus at the cricopharyngeus
Immediately below the squamocolumnar junction at the cardia (90% of cases)
Gastric antrum
Mid-esophagus beside the aortic arch
Duodenal bulb

concepts.title: Corrosive Injury of the Esophagus
concepts.summary_ar: يوضح هذا المفهوم إصابات الأكّال: القلويات عديمة الطعم والرائحة تُبتلع بأحجام كبيرة وتسبب انحلالا وتصبنا للدهون وخثارا للأوعية، بينما الحموض تسبب نخارا تخثريا بجلبة تحد العمق وتضر المعدة أكثر عبر التشنج البوابي، والتنظير المبكر مفتاح التدبير، والتضيق يصيب نحو نصف الإصابات الواسعة، ويؤجل القطع الانتخابي ثلاثة أشهر على الأقل.

sections.heading: Agents, Circumstances and Determinants of Injury
sections.body_text:
**Corrosives such as sodium hydroxide (lye, caustic soda) or sulphuric acid may be taken in attempted suicide.** Accidental ingestion occurs in **children** and when corrosives are **stored in bottles labeled as beverages** - the classic domestic-poisoning scenario.

**All corrosives can cause severe damage to the mouth, pharynx, larynx, esophagus and stomach.** The extent of damage is largely determined by three variables:
- The **type of agent** (alkali versus acid).
- Its **concentration**.
- The **volume ingested**.

Because the outcome ranges from trivial mucosal edema to transmural necrosis with perforation, grading of injury endoscopically drives every subsequent decision - nothing else predicts the phase of care as reliably.
key_points: Agents: sodium hydroxide (lye, caustic soda) and sulphuric acid; suicide attempts, childhood accidents, mislabeled beverage bottles.
Damage may involve mouth, pharynx, larynx, esophagus and stomach.
Extent depends on agent type, concentration and volume ingested.

sections.heading: Alkali versus Acid - Mechanisms of Injury
sections.body_text:
**Alkalis (sodium hydroxide, lye, caustic soda):**
- Are **relatively odorless and tasteless, making them more likely to be ingested in large volume** before the victim stops swallowing.
- Cause **liquefaction, saponification of fats, dehydration and thrombosis of blood vessels** - a progressively deepening injury that can traverse the entire wall and perforate.

**Acids (e.g., sulphuric acid):**
- Cause **coagulative necrosis with eschar formation**, and **this coagulant may limit penetration to deeper layers of the oesophageal wall** - the burn creates its own barrier.
- **Acids cause more gastric damage than alkalis because of the induction of intense pylorospasm with pooling in the antrum** - the corrosive bath is trapped against the antral mucosa.

Examination of the mouth and oropharynx does NOT predict the depth of esophageal injury; only endoscopy does.
key_points: Alkalis: odorless and tasteless - ingested in large volumes.
Alkali injury: liquefaction, saponification of fats, dehydration, vessel thrombosis - deep.
Acid injury: coagulative necrosis with eschar that may limit deeper penetration.
Acids cause more gastric damage: intense pylorospasm with pooling in the antrum.
Oral examination does not predict esophageal injury.

check.prompt: Why do ingested acids typically cause more GASTRIC damage than alkalis?
options: Acids are always ingested in larger volumes
Acids induce intense pylorospasm with pooling of the corrosive in the antrum
Acids saponify the gastric wall directly
Alkalis are tasteless so none of them reaches the stomach
The stomach completely neutralizes alkalis

sections.heading: Acute Management of Corrosive Injury
sections.body_text:
**The key to management is early endoscopy by an experienced endoscopist to inspect the whole of the oesophagus and stomach.** Endoscopy is performed once the airway is secure and the patient is resuscitated - usually within the first 24 hours - and it grades the burn from superficial to transmural.
- **Minor injuries with only oedema (edema) of the mucosa resolve rapidly with no late sequelae** - no stricture, no prolonged follow-up.
- **With more severe injuries, a feeding jejunostomy may be appropriate until the patient can swallow saliva satisfactorily** - enteral nutrition delivered beyond the burn, with serial reassessment of safe swallowing.
- **The widespread use of broad-spectrum antibiotics and steroids is controversial** - neither has convincingly prevented stricture or perforation; antibiotics are justified for proven infection or perforation, and steroids remain debated.
- **Emergency surgery is reserved for bleeding or perforation** during the acute necrotizing phase.

Neutralization, induced emesis and blind nasogastric intubation are avoided - each maneuver can add further injury.
key_points: Key to management: early endoscopy by an experienced endoscopist of the whole esophagus and stomach.
Minor injuries (mucosal edema only) resolve rapidly with no late sequelae.
Severe injuries: feeding jejunostomy until saliva is swallowed satisfactorily.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics and steroid use is controversial.
Emergency surgery only for bleeding or perforation.

sections.heading: Stricture Development and Timing of Elective Surgery
sections.body_text:
**Regular endoscopic examinations are the best way to assess stricture development** after corrosive injury - surveillance endoscopy tracks the evolution from sloughing to fibrosis.
- **Significant stricture formation occurs in about 50 per cent of patients with extensive mucosal damage** - the single most important late statistic of the disease.
- The lecture's radiology image - a barium swallow (oesophagogram) of a chronic corrosive stricture - shows a **long, irregular, severe narrowing with a 'string-like' appearance** as contrast passes through the fibrotic segment, while the proximal and distal portions appear relatively dilated compared to the strictured area.
- **Emergency surgery is for bleeding or perforation; elective oesophageal resection should be deferred for at least three months until the fibrotic phase is established.** Operating during the immature, inflamed, vascular phase of the first weeks invites disaster; waiting allows demarcation, nutritional optimization and accurate definition of the length to be resected or dilated.
- Established strictures are managed with an endoscopic dilation program (bougies or balloon); resection or bypass is reserved for failures and nondilatable long strictures. Chronic corrosive strictures also carry a long-term risk of squamous cell carcinoma.
key_points: Regular endoscopic examination is the best way to monitor stricture development.
Significant stricture forms in about 50% of extensive mucosal damage.
Barium swallow: long irregular 'string-like' narrowing.
Elective resection deferred at least three months until the fibrotic phase is established.
Emergency surgery only for bleeding or perforation.

check.prompt: A patient survives extensive caustic injury but develops a long fibrotic stricture. When should elective esophageal resection be scheduled?
options: Immediately, during the acute necrotizing phase
Within the first week
After at least three months, once the fibrotic phase is established
Only after five years of observation
Never - all corrosive strictures respond fully to a single dilation

concepts.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease: Definition, Pathophysiology, Complications and Full Management Pathway
concepts.summary_ar: يستعرض هذا المفهوم داء الارتجاع المعدي المريئي: تعريفه وأشكاله الفسيولوجية مقابل المرضية، وآليات ضعف العاصرة السفلية، والأعراض وعلامات الإنذار، والمضاعفات كالتهاب المريء التآكلي المسؤول عن 40-60 بالمئة من الأعراض والتضيق ومريء باريت مع برنامج المراقبة، ثم العلاج بنمط الحياة والدواء وجراحة نيسن والتقنيات داخل التجويف.

sections.heading: Definition, Physiologic versus Pathologic Reflux, and Pathophysiology
sections.body_text:
**The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) defines GERD as symptoms OR mucosal damage produced by the abnormal reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus.** The disease is **often chronic and relapsing**, and **complications of GERD may be seen in patients who lack typical symptoms** - the silent-reflux trap.

**Physiologic reflux** (in healthy individuals) is **postprandial, short-lived, asymptomatic and without nocturnal symptoms**; occasional episodes occur in healthy people and are **more common when awake and in the upright position than during sleep in the supine position**. **Pathologic reflux (GERD)** is defined by **symptoms**, **mucosal injury** and **nocturnal symptoms**.

**Pathophysiology.** The **primary barrier to gastroesophageal reflux is the lower esophageal sphincter, which normally works in conjunction with the diaphragm**; if the barrier is disrupted, acid goes from the stomach to the esophagus. Gastroesophageal reflux results from **transient relaxation or incompetence of the lower esophageal sphincter, or increased pressure within the stomach**.

**Factors contributing to gastroesophageal reflux:**
- **Increased gastric volume (post meals)**.
- **Position pushing gastric contents close to the gastroesophageal juncture (junction) - such as bending or lying down**.
- **Increased gastric pressure (obesity or tight clothing)**.
- **Hiatal hernia**, which disconnects the LES from its diaphragmatic support.

Poor esophageal clearance by secondary peristalsis, diminished salivary bicarbonate and delayed gastric emptying all lengthen mucosal acid exposure time.
key_points: ACG definition: symptoms OR mucosal damage from abnormal reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus.
Physiologic reflux: postprandial, short-lived, asymptomatic, no nocturnal symptoms; more common awake/upright than supine/asleep.
Pathologic reflux: symptoms, mucosal injury, nocturnal symptoms.
Mechanism: transient LES relaxation or incompetence, or increased intragastric pressure.
Contributing factors: increased gastric volume, position (bending/lying), increased gastric pressure (obesity/tight clothing), hiatal hernia.

sections.heading: Clinical Manifestations and Alarm Signs
sections.body_text:
**Typical manifestations of GERD:**
- **Heartburn after meals, while bending over, or recumbent** - the defining symptom.
- **Dyspepsia or indigestion**.
- **Regurgitation of sour materials into the mouth, pain with swallowing**.
- **Atypical chest pain** that can mimic cardiac disease.
- **Extraesophageal manifestations: asthma, laryngitis, chronic cough, sore throat with hoarseness**.

**Alarms (alarm signs/symptoms)** - any of these in a reflux patient demands endoscopy because they signal complications or neoplasia:
- **Dysphagia**
- **Early satiety**
- **GI bleeding**
- **Odynophagia**
- **Vomiting**
- **Weight loss**
- **Iron deficiency anemia**

The atypical symptom list of esophageal disease (globus, hoarseness, wheezing/stridor, dyspnea, apnea, halitosis, nausea and vomiting, hematemesis, dyspepsia) maps directly onto reflux presentations, which is why GERD must be considered in unexplained respiratory and ENT complaints.
key_points: Heartburn after meals, bending over, or recumbent; dyspepsia; sour regurgitation; pain with swallowing; atypical chest pain.
Extraesophageal: asthma, laryngitis, chronic cough, sore throat with hoarseness.
Alarm signs: dysphagia, early satiety, GI bleeding, odynophagia, vomiting, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia.

sections.heading: Complications: Erosive Esophagitis, Stricture and Barrett's - with Surveillance
sections.body_text:
GERD has three classical complications:

**1. Erosive esophagitis**
- **Responsible for 40-60 per cent of GERD symptoms.**
- **Severity of symptoms often fails to match severity of erosive esophagitis** - minimal heartburn with deep ulceration, or severe symptoms with an intact mucosa (non-erosive reflux disease). Symptom severity is therefore not a proxy for injury severity.

**2. Esophageal stricture**
- **Result of healing of erosive esophagitis** - fibrotic narrowing of the distal esophagus.
- Presents as progressive solid-food dysphagia and **may need dilation** (bougienage or balloon) combined with acid suppression.

**3. Barrett's esophagus**
- **Columnar metaplasia of the esophagus**: acid damages the lining and causes **chronic esophagitis**; the damaged area heals in a **metaplastic process in which abnormal columnar cells replace squamous cells**.
- **This specialized intestinal metaplasia can progress to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma** - Barrett's is the strongest known risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma.
- **Management of Barrett's esophagus: in the same manner as GERD**, plus surveillance - **EGD every 3 years in patients without dysplasia**, and **in patients with dysplasia, surveillance at annual to shorter intervals**.

**Which GERD patients need regular EGD?** Those with **alarm symptoms**, **poor therapeutic response**, or **long symptom duration**; a **'once in a lifetime' EGD for patients with chronic GERD is becoming accepted practice**, because **many patients with Barrett's are asymptomatic** and would otherwise never be detected.
key_points: Erosive esophagitis: responsible for 40-60% of GERD symptoms; symptom severity often mismatches injury severity.
Stricture: healing of erosive esophagitis; may need dilation.
Barrett's: columnar metaplasia replacing squamous epithelium; specialized intestinal metaplasia can progress to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma.
Barrett's without dysplasia: EGD every 3 years; with dysplasia: annual or shorter intervals.
Regular EGD for alarm symptoms, poor response, long duration; 'once in a lifetime' EGD for chronic GERD is accepted practice.
Many Barrett's patients are asymptomatic.

check.prompt: A patient with chronic GERD has biopsy-proven Barrett's esophagus WITHOUT dysplasia. What surveillance interval does the lecture recommend?
options: No further endoscopy is ever needed
EGD every 3 years
EGD every 3 months for life
Immediate esophagectomy
EGD only if alarm symptoms develop
